Photograph: Social media/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv’s forces hit Wildberries again amid deadly trade of strikes with Russia Drone attack on warehouse of Russian retailer triggers fire as at least 14 killed in cross-border exchanges; EU force boards Russian ‘shadow fleet’ tanker. What we know on day 1,622 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian drone strikes killed at least nine people in Russia on Sunday, with targets again including retail giant Wildberries, while Russian attacks on Ukraine killed at least five , according to officials in both countries. Drones attacked a Wildberries warehouse in the Samara region, about 800km (500 ​miles) from Ukraine’s most advanced military positions, governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev ‌said. There were ‌no casualties and a fire triggered by the attack was being put out, he said. Ukrainian forces have attacked about a dozen Wildberries sites since 18 July in an attempt to disrupt the operations of the company, which is Russia’s largest online retailer and a linchpin of the consumer economy often described as the country’s version of Amazon. Three people were killed and two injured in a drone attack on the Udmurtia region of Russia , acting governor Olga Abramova said. In the border region of ⁠Belgorod, three people were killed and five injured in Ukrainian strikes, the local taskforce reported. A Ukrainian drone struck an area next to ⁠a playground, killing one child and injuring two, acting regional governorAlexander Shuvayev said. Russian strikes in Ukraine killed two people in the eastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, and at least one person each in the southern regions of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, according to regional authorities. A separate Russian strike destroyed a postal terminal in the northern Kharkiv region, killing a worker, the mail operator Nova Poshta said. View image in fullscreen A police officer at the site of the Russian guided bomb attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA A strike on a Russian residential building in Samara’s neighbouring region of Saratov killed two people in the city of Engels , governor Roman Busargin ‌said. Civil infrastructure was damaged in Engels and the city of Saratov, he said. Ukraine’s military said on Sunday that their forces attacked the Saratov oil refinery and the Engels military airbase, sparking fires at both facilities. It said its forces also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region. Russia’s defence ​ministry said its forces struck infrastructure and two vessels with military cargo in the Ukrainian port of Mykolaiv, as well as a vessel carrying military supplies in the Black Sea. An EU naval mission led by Italy boarded a tanker from Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet” on Sunday, the ⁠second such operation in ⁠less than ​two weeks as Europe intensifies scrutiny of vessels suspected of helping Moscow circumvent oil sanctions. Italy’s defence ministry said the Toa Payoh, a ⁠tanker subject to EU sanctions, was intercepted west of the Sicilian island of Pantelleria while sailing from Benin to Istanbul. The vessel had switched to ⁠a Cameroon registry only last week, a source familiar with the operation said. http://www.bjreview.com.cn/China/202607/.text: Home | China | Opinion Governance Pacific Dialogue Fact Check Voice | World | Business | Lifestyle | Video Wisdom Without Borders Pacific Dialogue Through Their Eyes Real People, Real Lives On the Scene My China Eye | Multimedia Photography Infographics | Documents | Special Reports | Xinjiang Today Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with Slovak President Peter Pellegrini, who is on a state visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, on July 28 (XINHUA) Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks with Slovak President Peter Pellegrini in Beijing on July 28. China stands ready to join hands with Slovakia in forging a strategic partnership that features mutual respect and trust, equality and mutual benefit, as well as stability and resilience, Xi told Pellegrini, who is on a state visit to China. Xi stressed that mutual respect for each other's development paths and a firm commitment to friendship and cooperation have been the foundation for the sound and rapid growth of China-Slovakia relations. China commends Slovakia for upholding the one-China principle and will continue to work with Slovakia to accommodate each other's core interests and major concerns, he said. He called on the two countries to tap the potential for collaboration in emerging sectors and frontier fields, including clean energy, digital economy, robotics and AI, to create new highlights in bilateral cooperation. The two sides should broaden cooperation in culture, sports, tourism, youth and subnational exchanges, and make it easier for people to travel between the two countries, he said. Xi said China and Slovakia should safeguard the UN-centered international system and the international order underpinned by international law, jointly promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, and contribute to building a community with a shared future for humanity. China has always viewed the EU as a partner and develops its ties with the EU with sincerity and goodwill, Xi said, calling on Slovakia to play a constructive role in promoting the sound and steady growth of China-EU relations. Noting that Slovakia values the strategic partnership with China, Pellegrini expressed the expectation for more outcomes in cooperation in economy and trade, AI, digital economy, robotics and new energy. He added that Slovakia welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest there. As an EU member state, Slovakia is willing to actively promote cooperation between the EU and China and the proper settlement of differences through dialogue and consultation, said Pellegrini. Slovakia is willing to work with China to uphold multilateralism, safeguard the purposes of the UN Charter and international law, and promote regional and world peace and stability, he said, adding that his country is willing to closely coordinate with China to strengthen global governance of AI. Prior to the talks, Xi held a welcome ceremony for Pellegrini. A welcome banquet was also held for him around noon.

Photograph: Libkos/Getty Ukraine Russian strike on warehouse near Kyiv kills at least 37 Attack on business apparently storing ‘explosive objects’ sparks huge fire, damaging residential buildings Donna Ferguson Sat 29 Aug 2026 08.01 EDT First published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 07.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 37 people have been killed after a Russian drone struck a warehouse near Kyiv’s western suburbs which appears to have been storing “explosive objects”. The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings, including a care home for elderly and disabled people, and sparked a huge fire and explosions in the Bucha district of the Ukrainian capital. The regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said a further 42 people, including four children, had been injured after the Russian drone strike. More than 370 people have been evacuated from the area, and the evacuation process is still continuing, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said. In a statement, he said that a warehouse in the town of Myla had been struck “followed by a detonation”. He did not give details, but wrote in the same message that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence. “There are regulations in place – ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” Zelenskyy said. “As of now, 27 people have been reported killed. One of those killed was the head of the Dmytrivka community, Taras Didych. He was rescuing people,” he added. Ukrainian prosecutors said that after an unmanned aerial vehicle hit the grounds of an enterprise in Myla, “a large-scale fire broke out … and detonation began”. They have opened an investigation into the legality of the “storage of explosive objects and materials” on the enterprise’s grounds. The Ukrainian prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, expressed regret that mistakes had not been learned from a previous deadly strike on a munitions depot in Vyshneve , near Kyiv, in July. An investigation into that incident, in which 22 people were killed and fires tore through nearby homes, revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations on the proximity of residential buildings. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from a fire at a large warehouse storing car tires and wheels after a Russian strike in the Bucha district in the Kyiv region. Photograph: Libkos/Getty “Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson,” Koretskyi said. “In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again.” In a statement, Russia’s ministry of defence said that it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It also said that it had attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics centre and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region. Elsewhere, Russian attacks across Ukraine’s southern Kherson region killed two people and wounded 27 more on Saturday, including a child, a local official said. https://www.politico.eu/article/tiktok-b.text: BRUSSELS — The European Commission’s refusal to get on TikTok is facing pushback inside its Berlaymont HQ, with some officials arguing the EU is making a strategic mistake by staying off a platform used by around 200 million Europeans. The question of whether the executive should establish a presence on Chinese-owned TikTok has come up in high-level meetings, with at least one commissioner arguing for a rethink, according to an official granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, as were others spoken to for this article. The Commission banned TikTok from staff devices in 2023 over cybersecurity concerns. The ban also covers “personal devices enrolled in the Commission mobile device service,” a spokesperson for the institution said. Advertisement Advertisement “We follow the evolution of the platform, in particular the status of developments regarding data protection and cybersecurity concerns,” the Commission said. There is little sign the Commission’s policy is about to change. Dana Spinant, the Commission’s director-general for communications, opposes creating an official account, according to another official familiar with the discussions. Spinant did not respond to a request for comment. A third official said there was frustration in some commissioners’ cabinets that Brussels was absent from a platform where young Europeans increasingly derive their news and views. A second official argued that Russia has no such qualms about using social media platforms to influence European public opinion and that the Commission could not afford to cede ground. The debate comes as President Ursula von der Leyen and her commissioners are seeking to reach more Europeans using social media. Von der Leyen will invite influencers, including some who share content on TikTok, to her State of the Union speech this month. The third official called it ironic that the Commission is encouraging influencers to communicate its message on a platform while refusing to establish a presence there itself. The Commission is instead increasingly turning to YouTube, a U.S.-based platform where it has more than 500,000 subscribers, according to two of the officials.

https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/latest-.text: Andy Burnham is facing calls to take a military threat from Russia more seriously following warnings that Vladimir Putin may be plotting to strike the UK. Poland's Prime Minister revealed on Thursday evening that Russia is gearing up to launch missile strikes on countries supporting Ukraine . Donald Tusk issued the stark warning of escalating conflict after his nation was forced to close its airspace and airports amid the Kremlin's. Now experts in the UK are pleading with Prime Minister Andy Burnham to fully consider the danger posed by Russia. This morning (September 18), security correspondent Deborah Haynes wrote on X that the escalating warnings from Poland “would surely require the UK to be part of any response – collective or otherwise”. Elsewhere political commentator Tim Shipman said: “Time for the government here [in the UK] to say something?” Former Tory MP Simon Clarke, the director of the think tank Onward, said: “The Government cannot sustain its position on deferring *even setting out a plan* for increased defence spending until next year”. He added: "Things may be about to become very serious indeed - much more so than is widely appreciated." Mark Rutte, NATO chief, said that the UK needs a 'credible path' towards meeting its defence spending target with 'yearly increments'. If Russia was to launch missile strikes on British facilities, this would represent a dramatic escalation of the conflict. Russian drone attacks and reconnaissance missions within NATO airspace have occurred before, but not missile strikes. The aerial bombardment in Poland took place just days after a railway station close to the border was nearly struck by a high-speed jet-powered drone while Western officials including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson were on board. Mr Tusk told Polish MPs: "We know he is plotting something bad. However, for us the most important task is to prepare for various scenarios. "We will certainly not naively accept such messages that Russia has goodwill and will start behaving properly. There is no indication of this." Tusk continued, stating that the intelligence was 'very consistent and convincing', warning that Russia might portray future strikes as accidental. He further commented that Russia is looking to test NATO's resolve in an unprecedented way in the coming months.

By Monday, Trump offered an explanation for his assertion that both countries had agreed: “Because I said, ‘You agreed.’” WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump ’s energy ceasefire announcement was followed by Ukrainian reports of fresh Russian attacks on power facilities, while Moscow withheld public confirmation that it had accepted the arrangement. By Monday, Trump offered an explanation for his assertion that both countries had agreed: “Because I said, ‘You agreed.’” The exchange, reported by CNN, left Washington describing an agreement whose terms neither combatant had publicly confirmed before its announcement. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv supported reciprocal restraint but had been surprised by Trump’s declaration. The Kremlin subsequently said discussions were continuing. The dispute comes after decades of documented breaches involving Russia and forces it supported, from Abkhazia ’s broken ceasefire in 1993 to fighting in eastern Ukraine after the Minsk agreement in 2015. It also follows Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports while pressing Ukraine to suspend attacks on Russian refineries. Trump announced the proposed ceasefire on October 11, saying it would take effect immediately. Zelensky subsequently accused Russia of striking a power plant in Kharkiv and said Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian energy facilities during the two days following the announcement. According to the CNN report, Zelensky pledged reciprocal restraint if Russia stopped its attacks. Trump, meanwhile, said he believed Putin was ready to reach a settlement but expressed doubts about Zelensky’s willingness. Moscow had not publicly endorsed the ceasefire’s terms. On October 13, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said contacts concerning the proposal were continuing, without identifying the participants or describing an agreement. Russia’s Defense Ministry said its overnight operations had not targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, according to Reuters’ account of the Kremlin’s response . r Ukraine’s allegations concern attacks after Trump’s declaration. Public confirmation that Moscow had accepted a defined agreement remained absent. The civilian toll has continued to rise. The United Nations’ August assessment recorded at least 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured in Ukraine that month. Its verified January–August totals were 2,222 killed and 13,058 injured. Ukraine’s earlier agreements Russia’s commitments to Ukraine extend beyond battlefield truces. Under the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Moscow provided security assurances connected to Ukraine’s surrender of its inherited nuclear arsenal, including respect for its sovereignty and existing borders. Russia seized and annexed Crimea in 2014, then backed armed separatists in eastern Ukraine. Its full-scale invasion began in February 2022. Ukraine has repeatedly cited those actions in rejecting the adequacy of its earlier security assurances. A particularly well-documented ceasefire breach occurred around Debaltseve in February 2015, after the Minsk II agreement. In a contemporaneous monitoring report , the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe recorded that Ukrainian military representatives said they were willing to cease fire. Representatives of the Russian-backed separatist entities were unwilling, the monitors reported, in clear contravention of their earlier agreement. The European Union’s foreign policy chief, Federica Mogherini, separately called the separatists’ actions in Debaltseve a clear violation of the ceasefire. Abkhazia: the broken Sochi ceasefire The relevant Sochi agreement for Abkhazia was signed on July 27, 1993, during Boris Yeltsin’s presidency, years before Putin became Russia’s leader. It established a ceasefire and arrangements for monitoring compliance. On September 16, Russia and Russia supported militants broke the ceasefire and launched an offensive. Sukhumi fell on September 27. In Resolution 876, the U.N. Security Council condemned the Abkhaz side’s grave violation of the July agreement and demanded an end to violations of international humanitarian lawm while Georgian President blamed Russia for an offensive. Russia’s military involvement was documented separately by Human Rights Watch’s investigation. It found that Russian aircrafts and Black Sea fleet bombed civilian targets in Georgian-controlled territory and Russian military vessels, operated by supporters of the Abkhaz side, were made available to shell Georgian-held Sukhumi. The investigation also documented Russian weapons reaching Abkhaz forces and Russian-trained, Russian-paid fighters operating in Tkvarcheli. Foreign fighters came principally from neighboring Russian regions; whether particular participants were mercenaries or volunteers varied. Moscow officially maintained neutrality, and its Foreign Ministry condemned the September offensive. The subsequent expulsion of ethnic Georgians received explicit international recognition. The 1994 Budapest summit declaration, adopted by the organization then called the CSCE, expressed deep concern over ethnic cleansing, the mass expulsion of predominantly Georgian residents and civilian deaths. A U.N. fact-finding mission documented executions, torture, forced displacement and other abuses, with responsibility extending to forces on both sides. The Security Council later condemned attempts to alter Abkhazia’s demographic composition in Resolution 896. Concessions to Moscow, pressure on Kyiv Trump has continued to say Putin wants peace. But Reuters reported that American envoys told Ukrainian officials in Miami that Putin was not prepared to negotiate an end to the war and that the diesel arrangement might help bring him back to talks. The envoys also reiterated Washington’s request that Ukraine stop attacking Russian refineries. Ukrainian participants viewed the approach skeptically, according to Reuters’ reporting on the meeting. Now It Is Holding It Shut The Russian diesel dispute has also produced bipartisan objections in Congress. Lawmakers cited the statutory restrictions imposed on Russian energy imports after the invasion and warned against providing Moscow additional revenue. On October 13, Trump defended the arrangement and said American intelligence-sharing with Ukraine continued. Asked whether Russia could use the proceeds to buy more bombs, he said the diesel was being released into world markets, according to Reuters . Data-center strikes and the bot claims Ukrainian attacks on three Yandex data centers have prompted claims that Russian propaganda activity collapsed. Zelensky said social media had become less hostile after the strikes. Independent reporting has drawn a narrower conclusion. Euronews reported a sharp decline in automated traffic from Yandex’s network, but that traffic included legitimate search-engine crawlers. Experts interviewed by BBC Verify said there was no evidence of a significant reduction in Russian influence networks. Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation reported temporary disruptions in specific propaganda networks. It said posting volume in certain clusters fell by approximately half for around 12 hours before recovering, while acknowledging a lack of evidence for a significant overall decline in Russian bot activity. Those preliminary Ukrainian findings have not been independently verified. Russia’s documented election operations American investigations provide a separate record of Russian influence efforts. In 2018, federal prosecutors charged 13 Russian nationals and three companies over an alleged operation to interfere in American politics, including the 2016 election. A separate indictment accused 12 Russian intelligence officers of hacking Democratic organizations and releasing stolen material. United States Department of Justice In September 2024, the Justice Department announced the seizure of 32 domains associated with the Doppelganger influence operation . Prosecutors alleged that companies operating under the Russian presidential administration’s direction sought to influence voters, weaken international support for Ukraine and promote Russian interests through impersonated news sites, fabricated identities and manipulated content. United States Department of Justice Public doubts, and the limits of the polling Trump’s approach to Ukraine has faced measurable public skepticism. A Pew Research Center survey, conducted August 4–10, 2025, among 3,554 adults, found 59 percent lacked confidence in his decisions about the war; 40 percent expressed confidence. Thirty-three percent said he favored Russia too much, compared with 6 percent who said he favored Ukraine too much. The share saying he favored Russia excessively had declined from 43 percent in March 2025, while uncertainty increased. Confidence in his handling of the war nevertheless fell from 45 percent in July 2024 to 40 percent in August 2025. More recently, Reuters/Ipsos recorded overall presidential approval at 32 percent in its September 30–October 5, 2026, survey. Reuters reported that living costs were voters’ leading election concern. The survey preceded the latest ceasefire announcement; it provides no measurement of that episode’s effect on approval.
